topic: Operating Rules, Speed, and No-Wake Zones
question: A capacity plate, required by the USCG on most monohull boats less than 20 feet, generally shows:
choice_b: The maximum recommended horsepower, number of persons, and/or weight the vessel can safely carry
explanation: A federally required capacity plate tells an operator the maximum safe horsepower, person count, and/or weight capacity for that specific boat, information critical to avoiding a dangerous overload.
source_note: Standard USCG capacity-plate requirement used across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

topic: Operating Rules, Speed, and No-Wake Zones
question: An operator whose excessive wake damages a moored boat or dock, even in an area without a posted no-wake sign, is generally:
choice_a: Still potentially liable, since the general safe-speed and due-care standard applies regardless of posted signage
choice_b: Automatically excused from any responsibility because no sign was posted
choice_c: Only liable if the damaged boat was also underway at the time
choice_d: Immune from liability as long as the operator was under the vessel's top speed
explanation: Louisiana's general safe-speed and due-care operating standard applies everywhere, not just in posted no-wake zones, so an operator whose wake damages a moored vessel or dock can still be held responsible even without a sign present.
source_note: LDWF, Boating Regulations (wlf.louisiana.gov/page/boating-regulations), applying the general safe-speed/due-care standard

topic: Operating Rules, Speed, and No-Wake Zones
question: A low-head dam poses a particular danger to boaters because it can create:
choice_a: A recirculating hydraulic "keeper" current on its downstream side that can trap and hold even a strong swimmer or a boat
choice_c: A permanent no-wake zone with no other hazard
choice_d: A safe area to anchor overnight
explanation: The recirculating hydraulic current below a low-head dam can trap swimmers and boats in a way that is often underestimated even by experienced boaters, which is why such structures should be avoided entirely rather than approached closely.
source_note: Standard low-head dam hazard fundamentals used across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

topic: Operating Rules, Speed, and No-Wake Zones
question: While a vessel is underway, passengers should generally:
choice_a: Ride on the bow, gunwales, seatbacks, or transom whenever there is room to do so
choice_b: Remain properly seated inside the vessel, since a sudden wake or maneuver can throw an improperly seated passenger overboard
choice_c: Stand up near the stern to improve visibility
choice_d: Sit on the transom edge for a better view of the wake
explanation: Passengers riding on the bow, gunwales, seatbacks, or transom risk being thrown overboard by a sudden wake, wake-jump, or hard maneuver, so proper seating inside the vessel is part of safe operating practice.
source_note: Standard passenger-seating safety fundamentals used across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

topic: Operating Rules, Speed, and No-Wake Zones
question: Leaving the helm unattended while a vessel is underway and on plane is risky primarily because:
choice_a: Most vessels are not designed to hold a straight, safe course indefinitely without operator input, and a sudden turn or hazard could go unaddressed
choice_b: It has no effect since modern outboards always travel in a perfectly straight line
choice_c: It is only a concern for sailboats, never powerboats
choice_d: Leaving the helm briefly is required by law during refueling
explanation: A powerboat underway generally will not reliably hold a safe course on its own, so an unattended helm at speed leaves no one able to react to a hazard, another vessel, or a sudden course change.
source_note: Standard safe-operating fundamentals used across NASBLA-aligned boating courses
